title: Water birds of the river

names.gloss: sentry bird which warns of crocodiles along the banks of the river

identification.basis: The dictionary's water-bird words are by habit and colour: white crane, spoonbill, straw-necked ibis, black diver bird, seashore plover, and the sentry bird that warns of crocodiles. The species here are the ones the Atlas records within 30 km of Karma Waters: pelican, two cormorants, darter, four herons and egrets, two ibises, spoonbill, jabiru, jacana, grebe, coot, lapwing and dotterel.

summary: The dictionary names the water birds by what they do: **[dulku](word:dulku)** the 'white crane', which is the egret; **[biluwarra](word:biluwarra)** the 'spoon bill bird'; **[birmba](word:birmba)** the 'straw-necked ibis'; **[kalmbangarr](word:kalmbangarr)** the 'black diver bird', the cormorant or darter; **[juril-juril](word:juril-juril)** the 'seashore plover'; and **[kurrujuwa](word:kurrujuwa)**, the 'sentry bird which warns of crocodiles along the banks of the river' [ref:hershberger1982]. The pools of the Mitchell at [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) carry the whole set: the pelican, fifteen records within 30 km, the darter and two cormorants, the great egret and three herons, the straw-necked and white ibises, the royal spoonbill, the black-necked stork or jabiru, the jacana walking the lily pads, the grebe, the coot, the masked lapwing and the dotterel on the sand [ref:ala-aves]. Each works a different depth and hour: the darter and cormorants under the water for fish, the egrets and herons stalking the edge by day, the night heron the same edge by night, the ibis and spoonbill the mud, the jabiru the deep shallows for the big fish, the pelican the open pool in a line [ref:wiki-darter] [ref:wiki-white-necked-heron] [ref:wiki-night-heron] [ref:wiki-spoonbill] [ref:am-stork] [ref:wiki-pelican]. Roth's hunters took them 'in the nesting season by sneaking upon them unawares', and at Boulia lured the pelican by throwing empty mussel shells on the water 'to some considerable distance' until the bird, thinking them jumping fish, swam within reach of a boomerang [ref:roth1901]. The sentry bird is the one to learn first.

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **[dulku](word:dulku)** 'white crane', which is how the great egret and the other white egrets were named in English too. **[biluwarra](word:biluwarra)** 'spoon bill bird'. **[birmba](word:birmba)** 'straw-necked ibis', also **[bujil-yiran](word:bujil-yiran)**. **[kalmbangarr](word:kalmbangarr)** 'black diver bird', the cormorants and the darter. **[juril-juril](word:juril-juril)** 'seashore plover', the lapwings and dotterels of the sand. **[kurrujuwa](word:kurrujuwa)** 'sentry bird which warns of crocodiles along the banks of the river'; the dictionary does not say which bird, and the masked lapwing, which 'is always alert and, even though it rests, it never sleeps properly', and gives its 'warning call' at anything that moves on the bank, is the obvious candidate [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:wiki-lapwing]. **[bidu-bidu](word:bidu-bidu)** 'bank bird'; **[dikal](word:dikal)** 'bird'; **[diwalngku](word:diwalngku)** 'migratory bird' [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: The water birds of the upper Mitchell
sections.body:
**Pelican** (*Pelecanus conspicillatus*), fifteen records. 'Medium-sized by pelican standards, with a wingspan of 2.3 to 2.6 m. Weight can range from 4 to 13 kg'; 'predominantly white in colour', the pouch pink and turning 'dark blue, pink and scarlet' in courtship. 'Australian pelicans occur primarily in large expanses of open water without dense aquatic vegetation ... large lakes, reservoirs, billabongs and rivers'; they 'follow no particular schedule of regular movement, simply following the availability of food supplies' [ref:wiki-pelican]. Roth's Boulia method: the hunter 'will sit in the water, in ambush, under cover of the bushes or suitable overhanging tree, etc., and throw empty mussel shells one after another to some considerable distance in the water. The bird, thinking that these are fish "jumping" on the surface, comes closer to inspect: at the same time the concealed and otherwise immoveable individual taps the water with his fingers to mimic fish splashing ... and, when arrived close enough, is either hit with a boomerang or sometimes even caught with the hands' [ref:roth1901].

**Darter** (*Anhinga novaehollandiae*), twenty-seven records. 'A slim bird measuring 86–94 cm long with a snakelike slender neck. The male has black plumage with a white streak down the side of its head and neck, while the female has white underparts.' 'Typical habitat is freshwater or brackish wetlands more than 0.5 m deep with fallen trees or logs and vegetated banks'. 'The Australasian darter forages in water, often with only its head and neck exposed. Its feathers soak up water in spaces between them, allowing the bird to reduce its natural buoyancy and swim underwater. It eats a wide variety of fish such as Australian smelt, bony bream' and has been photographed 'eating a northern saratoga' [ref:wiki-darter].

**Cormorants.** The little pied cormorant (*Microcarbo melanoleucos*), nineteen records, 'a small cormorant measuring 56–58 cm', black above and white below, 'a benthic feeder, i.e. it finds its prey on the sea floor. It is a solitary feeder, normally diving in relatively shallow water, often near the shore. Dive times are short, around 15 to 20 seconds', and it takes a high proportion of crayfish and prawns [ref:wiki-little-pied-cormorant] [ref:am-little-pied-cormorant]. The little black cormorant (*Phalacrocorax sulcirostris*), seventeen records, 'measuring 60–65 cm with all black plumage', 'more gregarious than other cormorants ... can be found in large flocks', 'feeds mainly on fish' and fishes as a flock, driving the shoals [ref:wiki-little-black-cormorant].

**Herons and egrets.** The great egret (*Ardea alba*, *dulku*), twenty-nine records, 'a large, widely distributed' white heron that stalks the shallows; the intermediate egret, eight [ref:wiki-great-egret] [ref:ala-aves]. The white-necked heron (*Ardea pacifica*), twenty-eight, 'a large, diurnal, long-legged waterbird ... mostly slate-grey to black with distinctive black spots in the centre of the lower fore-neck and throat', with 'an elongated neck and beak designed to reach out and catch fish, frogs, spiders and other food animals'; 'nomadic like most water birds in Australia, moving from one water source' to the next [ref:wiki-white-necked-heron]. The white-faced heron (*Egretta novaehollandiae*), twenty-eight, 'medium-sized, pale, slightly bluish-grey, with yellow legs and white facial markings', 'almost anywhere near shallow water, fresh or salt', 550 g and 60–70 cm [ref:wiki-white-faced-heron]. The nankeen night heron (*Nycticorax caledonicus*), eight, 'a medium-sized heron', 55–65 cm, rufous-backed with a black cap and 'a heavy black bill', which roosts in the river trees by day and fishes the edges by night [ref:wiki-night-heron].

**Ibises and spoonbill.** The straw-necked ibis (*Threskiornis spinicollis*, *birmba*), thirty-seven records, the commonest water bird in the Karma Waters list: 'large birds, around 59–76 cm long, with a bare black head and a long, downcurved black bill. They have a distinctive, highly iridescent plumage', with straw-yellow plumes on the neck; 'found around shallow freshwater wetlands, cultivated pastures, edges of swamps and lagoons, and wet or dry grasslands ... extremely nomadic', and a famous grasshopper-eater of the paddocks [ref:wiki-straw-necked-ibis]. The Australian white ibis (*T. molucca*), twelve, 'around 65–75 cm long and has a bald black head and neck and a long black downcurved beak', with 'a long croak' [ref:wiki-white-ibis]. The royal spoonbill (*Platalea regia*, *biluwarra*), seven, 'a large, white bird with a black, spoon-shaped bill ... approximately 80 cm tall', which feeds by 'sweeping its bill through shallow water and swallowing prey once detected', the bill 'open about 2 to 4 cm, sweeping an arc of around 100 degrees in front of the bird' [ref:wiki-spoonbill].

**Jabiru**, the black-necked stork (*Ephippiorhynchus asiaticus*), five records. 'A large bird, 110–137 cm tall having a 190–218 cm wingspan', black-and-white with an iridescent black neck and red legs, photographed in Queensland 'with a small barramundi'; it hunts the shallows for fish, eels, frogs and crabs and builds a big stick nest in a tall tree [ref:wiki-stork] [ref:am-stork].

**The small ones.** The comb-crested jacana (*Irediparra gallinacea*), twenty-two records, 'the lotusbird or lilytrotter', which 'eats seeds and aquatic insects gleaned from floating vegetation on the water surface' [ref:wiki-jacana]. The Australasian grebe (*Tachybaptus novaehollandiae*), nine, 'a small waterbird common on fresh water lakes and rivers', which 'if disturbed ... will dive and re-surface 10–15 metres away rather than fly' and carries its chicks on its back [ref:wiki-grebe]. The Eurasian coot (*Fulica atra*), eighteen, black with a white bill and shield, 'a noisy bird with a wide repertoire of crackling, explosive, or trumpeting calls, often given at night' [ref:wiki-coot]. The masked lapwing (*Vanellus miles*), twenty-three, 'a large, common and conspicuous bird' with 'a conspicuous yellow spur on the carpal joint of each wing', which 'spends most of its time on the ground searching for food such as insects and worms', nests on bare ground and 'has a wide range of calls which can be heard at any time of the day or night: the warning call, a loud defending call' [ref:wiki-lapwing]. The black-fronted dotterel (*Elseyornis melanops*), eleven, 16–18 cm, 'a distinct black face mask, forehead and v-shaped band across the chest', which 'live[s] along the edges of freshwater sources' and forages 'in a series of short running motions' [ref:wiki-dotterel].

sections.heading: Telling them at a distance
sections.body:
- **Darter**: swims with only the snake neck showing, spears fish, dries its wings spread on a snag; a long fan tail [ref:wiki-darter].
- **Cormorants**: swim low, dive from the surface, sit on snags with wings out; the pied one has a white front, the black one is black and fishes in flocks [ref:wiki-little-pied-cormorant] [ref:wiki-little-black-cormorant].
- **Egrets**: white, stalking; the great egret with a kinked neck as long as its body [ref:wiki-great-egret].
- **White-necked heron**: dark body, white neck, spotted throat; **white-faced heron**: blue-grey with a white face and yellow legs [ref:wiki-white-necked-heron] [ref:wiki-white-faced-heron].
- **Night heron**: hunched, rufous and black-capped, in the trees by day [ref:wiki-night-heron].
- **Ibises**: a curved black bill; the straw-necked with a dark glossy back, the white ibis white [ref:wiki-straw-necked-ibis] [ref:wiki-white-ibis].
- **Spoonbill**: white with a black spoon, sweeping [ref:wiki-spoonbill].
- **Jabiru**: huge, black-and-white, red legs, alone [ref:wiki-stork].
- **[Cranes](entry:brolga-and-cranes)**: grey with a red head, flying with the neck straight; the herons fold theirs [ref:wiki-brolga].
- **Jacana**: walking on the lily pads on enormous toes; **grebe**: a small diver that vanishes; **coot**: black with a white bill; **lapwing**: yellow face and wing spurs, screaming; **dotterel**: tiny, running on the sand [ref:wiki-jacana] [ref:wiki-grebe] [ref:wiki-coot] [ref:wiki-lapwing] [ref:wiki-dotterel].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **The sentry bird's call** on the bank, *kurrujuwa*: something is moving in the water or on the bank [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:wiki-lapwing].
- **Birds working one pool hard** in the late dry: the fish are concentrated there; the cormorants and darter show where the [spangled perch](entry:spangled-perch) are [ref:lintermans2023].
- **A darter spread-eagled on a snag** drying its wings [ref:wiki-darter].
- **A white egret at a crocodile's back**, picking the insects; and an egret that will not go near one end of a pool [ref:crocwise].
- **Mussel-shell piles** opened by birds on a bank; see [mussels](entry:mussels) [ref:wiki-azure-kingfisher].
- **A stick nest the size of a table** in a tall river tree: the jabiru [ref:wiki-stork].
- **Night-heron croaks** over the camp after dark [ref:wiki-night-heron].

sections.heading: Where they are
sections.body: The long dry-season pools of the Mitchell and the lagoons off it, the sand and mud edges, the snags, and the paperbark and gum fringe where the darter, the herons and the night heron roost and nest [ref:re9314]. The [waterhole](entry:waterhole) page has the pools' year; the straw-necked ibis and the lapwing are as much on the paddocks and burnt flats as on the water [ref:wiki-straw-necked-ibis] [ref:wiki-lapwing].

sections.heading: Who fishes when
sections.body: The pool is fished in shifts. By day the darter and the cormorants are under it, taking bony bream, [spangled perch](entry:spangled-perch), rainbowfish and small [saratoga](entry:saratoga), the pied cormorant more prawns and [cherabin](entry:cherabin); the egrets and herons stand the edge for small fish and frogs; the ibis and spoonbill work the mud for the insects, snails and crayfish; the jabiru takes the [eels](entry:eels), the big fish and the [turtles'](entry:freshwater-turtle) hatchlings; the pelicans fish the open water in a line [ref:wiki-darter] [ref:wiki-little-pied-cormorant] [ref:wiki-white-necked-heron] [ref:wiki-spoonbill] [ref:am-stork] [ref:wiki-pelican] [ref:jardine2012]. After dark the night heron takes the edge and the [mouth almighty](entry:mouth-almighty), the [sleepy cod](entry:sleepy-cod) and the prawns come out under it [ref:wiki-night-heron]. The [freshwater crocodile](entry:freshwater-crocodile) takes the birds that come too close, the [sea eagle and the kites](entry:woodland) take the chicks and the injured, and the [goanna](entry:goanna) takes the ground nests; the lapwing's spurs and screaming are against all three [ref:wiki-lapwing] [ref:wiki-wedgie]. The late dry, when the pools shrink and the fish are crowded, is when every one of these birds is on the river at once, and the shrinking is why they are here [ref:griffith2021].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: Nesting with the wet, in colonies in the river trees and reeds, which is 'the nesting season' of Roth's note; the birds spread across the flooded country then and come back to the pools as they shrink, until the late dry crowds them all together [ref:roth1901] [ref:griffith2021]. The nomads, the ibis, the white-necked heron and the pelican, come and go with the water across the north [ref:wiki-straw-necked-ibis] [ref:wiki-white-necked-heron] [ref:wiki-pelican]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- **Meat and eggs**, taken 'in the nesting season by sneaking upon them unawares' [ref:roth1901].
- **The pelican**, lured with mussel shells and taken with a boomerang or by hand [ref:roth1901].
- **Feathers**: the egret's plumes and the pelican's for ornament; the spear-decorating feathers of the camp [ref:anderson1996].
- **Fish-finders**: the birds show where the fish are concentrated [ref:lintermans2023].
- **Sentries**: the lapwing's alarm is the crocodile warning the dictionary names [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Reading the water birds
sections.body:
1. **Listen to the sentry.** When the *kurrujuwa* on the bank starts up and will not stop, look at the water before you look at anything else [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:wiki-lapwing].
2. **Follow the cormorants** to the fish; a flock of little black cormorants driving a pool is a shoal of [spangled perch](entry:spangled-perch) or bony bream in it [ref:wiki-little-black-cormorant].
3. **Watch the egrets' line**: the shallows they stand in are the shallows the fish use at dusk, and where to set a [trap](entry:fish-traps) [ref:wiki-great-egret].
4. **For a pelican**, Roth's lure: sit still in cover and throw mussel shells out, farther then nearer, tapping the water; the bird comes to the 'jumping fish' [ref:roth1901].
5. **Eggs** from the colony in the wet, leaving most; the colonies are small on an inland river [ref:roth1901].
6. **Never under a jabiru's tree** in the breeding season; the bird is big and the nest is its own.

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- Native birds are protected wildlife in Queensland under the *Nature Conservation Act 1992*; native title holders hunting for personal, domestic or non-commercial communal needs are covered by section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993*, recognised in the Western Yalanji determinations [ref:qld-nca] [ref:alrc] [ref:wyac2020].
- Water-bird country is crocodile country; the egret at the water's edge is not a sign that the edge is safe [ref:crocwise] [ref:kw-about].
- A jabiru's bill and a pelican's are weapons; a cornered bird strikes at the eyes.
- The night heron croaking over the camp is not an omen; the lapwing screaming at 2 a.m. is usually a dingo.

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: The straw-necked ibis, the egret, the darter and the lapwing are on the Karma Waters pools every day of the dry, and the jabiru is on the big lagoons; the station's river camps look straight at them [ref:ala-aves] [ref:kw-camping]. Which bird the Western Yalanji call the sentry, and the names of the rest, are for the contribution box below [ref:hershberger1982].
